title: Data Security

toc.title: The Four A's (+ E) of Security

html:
1Definition and Goals

Definition: Planning, development, and execution of security policies and procedures to provide proper authentication, authorization, access, and auditing of data and information assets.

Primary Goal: Protect information assets in alignment with privacy and confidentiality regulations, contractual agreements, and business requirements.

3 Goals:

  1. Enable appropriate access; prevent inappropriate access to enterprise data assets
  2. Understand and comply with all relevant regulations and policies for privacy, protection, confidentiality
  3. Ensure privacy and confidentiality needs of all stakeholders are enforced and audited

2Business Drivers

Two Primary Drivers:

  1. Risk Reduction — regulatory compliance, fiduciary responsibility, reputation protection
  2. Business Growth — trusted e-commerce drives profit; robust security builds customer confidence

Key Principle — "Goldilocks Principle": Data security must be appropriate — not too lax, not so onerous it prevents users from doing legitimate work.

Security as an Asset: Security Metadata (classifications) travels with data across the enterprise; enables standard enforcement across departments and reduces cost.

Four-Step Information Security Process:

  1. Identify and classify sensitive data assets
  2. Locate sensitive data throughout the enterprise
  3. Determine how each asset needs to be protected
  4. Identify how information interacts with business processes

3Six Guiding Principles

  1. Collaboration — involves IT security, data stewards, governance, audit, and legal
  2. Enterprise Approach — standards applied consistently across entire organization
  3. Proactive Management — dynamic, engage all stakeholders, overcome cultural bottlenecks
  4. Clear Accountability — roles defined; includes chain of custody for data
  5. Metadata-Driven — security classification is essential part of data definitions
  6. Reduce Risk by Reducing Exposure — minimize sensitive data proliferation, especially to non-production environments

4Essential Security Concepts

Vulnerability

Weakness allowing successful attack; examples: unpatched systems, weak passwords, untrained users, backdoors.

Threat

Potential offensive action against the organization; internal or external, malicious or unintentional. Also called attack surface.

Risk

Both the possibility of loss AND the condition posing potential loss.

  • Prioritized by: probability, damage type/amount, revenue effect, fix cost, prevention cost, attacker intent

Risk Classifications (3 Types)

Classification Description
Critical Risk Data (CRD) Personal info aggressively sought; high direct financial value; harm to individuals and company
High Risk Data (HRD) Actively sought; provides competitive edge; exposure causes financial harm, legal exposure
Moderate Risk Data (MRD) Little tangible value to outsiders; but unauthorized use has negative effect on company

Key Rule: Highest security classification of any datum in a data set determines the classification of the entire aggregation.

5The Four A's (+ E) of Security

Process Definition
Access Enable authorized individuals to connect to information systems in a timely manner
Audit Review security actions and user activity; ensure compliance with regulations and policy
Authentication Validate users' identities (passwords, tokens, biometrics); all transmissions encrypted
Authorization Grant individuals privileges to access specific data views appropriate to their role
Entitlement Sum total of all data elements exposed to user by a single access authorization decision

Monitoring Types:

  • Active Monitoring — real-time; detects unexpected events; alerts or interrupts suspicious activity (detection mechanism)
  • Passive Monitoring — tracks changes by snapshots; compares trends against benchmarks (assessment mechanism)

6Data Confidentiality Levels (5 Levels)

Level Description
For General Audiences Available to anyone, including the public
Internal Use Only Limited to employees; minimal risk if shared; not for copying outside organization
Confidential Not shared outside without NDA; client confidential data not shared with other clients
Restricted Confidential Limited to roles with 'need to know'; may require clearance
Registered Confidential Anyone accessing must sign legal agreement; highest secrecy

Key: Any data set can have only ONE confidentiality level, based on the most sensitive item within it.

7Regulatory Categories

Key Distinction — Confidentiality vs. Regulatory:

  • Confidentiality: restriction originates internally; one level per data set
  • Regulatory: externally defined; additive — a single data set may have multiple regulatory categories

Key Regulatory Families

Category Key Regulation(s)
PII (Personally Identifiable Information) EU Privacy Directives, PIPEDA (Canada), PIP Act (Japan), PCI, FTC, GLB
Financially Sensitive Data SOX (restricts who can change financial data), Insider Trading Laws (who can see it), GLBA
PHI (Personal Health Information) HIPAA (US)
Educational Records FERPA (US — Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act)
PCI-DSS Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard — credit card data, account numbers

SOX vs. Insider Trading Law: SOX restricts who can change financial data; Insider Trading Laws affect who can see it.

8Encryption

Definition: Process of translating plain text into complex codes to hide privileged information, verify transmission, or verify sender identity.

Three Main Encryption Methods

Method Key Facts
Hash Algorithms (MD5, SHA) convert data to mathematical representation; used for transmission integrity verification
Private-Key (Symmetric) One key for both encryption/decryption; algorithms: DES, 3DES, AES, IDEA, Twofish, Serpent
Public-Key (Asymmetric) Sender uses public key; receiver uses private key; methods: RSA, Diffie-Hellman; PGP = free application

9Data Masking / Obfuscation

Definition: Makes data less available by removing, shuffling, or changing appearance without losing meaning or relational integrity.

Two Masking Types

Type Key Facts
Persistent Permanently and irreversibly alters data; used between production and non-production environments
Dynamic Changes appearance to end user without changing underlying data; e.g., showing SSN as *--6789

Persistent Sub-types:

  • In-Flight Masking — data masked while moving (source → destination); more secure; re-runnable
  • In-Place Masking — source and destination same; overwrites unmasked data; risky if process fails mid-way

8 Masking Methods

Method Description
Substitution Replace with values from lookup/pattern
Shuffling Swap values within records or between rows
Temporal Variance Move dates +/– days (small enough to preserve trends)
Value Variance Apply random +/– percent factor
Nulling / Deleting Remove data not needed in test system
Randomization Replace with random characters or single character
Encryption Convert to unrecognizable character stream via cipher
Expression Masking Change all values to result of expression

Key Masking: 9th method — ensures result must be unique and repeatable; used for database key fields.

10Network Security Terms

Term Definition
Backdoor Hidden entry bypassing password requirement; any backdoor is a security risk
Bot / Zombie Workstation taken over remotely via Trojan/virus/phish; used for spam, attacks, money transfers
Bot-Net Network of infected machines
Cookie Small data file installed by website; identifies returning visitors; raises privacy concerns
Firewall Software/hardware filtering network traffic; most primitive form of IPS
Perimeter Boundary between organization's environment and exterior
DMZ (De-Militarized Zone) Edge area with firewall on both sides (between internet and organization)
Super User Account Admin/root access; emergency use only; credentials tightly controlled
Key Logger Attack software recording all keystrokes; sends data to hacker
Penetration Testing Ethical hacker attempts to break in; identifies vulnerabilities before release
VPN Uses internet to create encrypted secure tunnel into organization

11System Security Risks

Risk Description
Abuse of Excessive Privilege Users with more access than needed; mitigated by query-level access control
Abuse of Legitimate Privilege Users misuse valid access (intentional or accidental); mitigated by endpoint access control
Unauthorized Privilege Elevation Exploiting vulnerabilities to gain admin rights; mitigated by IPS + query access control
Service/Shared Account Abuse Batch/generic IDs untraceable to specific users; mitigated by strict management
Platform Intrusion Attacks Require software patches + IPS; firewalls alone insufficient for web environments
SQL Injection Injecting unauthorized SQL into data channels; mitigated by sanitizing inputs
Default Passwords Known to hackers; eliminate ALL default passwords after every implementation
Backup Data Abuse Backups represent security risk; encrypt all database backups

12Malware Types

Malware Description
Adware Monitors browsing habits; not illegal; easily leveraged for identity theft
Spyware Tracks online activity without consent; piggybacks on other software
Trojan Horse Malicious program disguised within legitimate software; installs malware, key loggers
Virus Attaches to executable file; needs host program; executes when infected file opens
Worm Self-reproduces/spreads across network; consumes bandwidth; can shut down network

Social Threats:

  • Phishing — call, IM, or email luring victims to reveal private info; often appear from legitimate sources
  • Spear-Phishing — targeted to specific senior executives by name
  • Social Engineering — hackers trick people into giving access by collecting info from multiple contacts

13Activities

Activity 1: Identify Data Security Requirements

  • Analyze business rules/processes to identify security touch points
  • Use data-to-process and data-to-role matrices (CRUD)
  • Create central inventory of all relevant regulations

Activity 2: Define Data Security Policy

  • Based on business and regulatory requirements
  • Requires collaboration: IT security, security architects, data governance, data stewards, audit, legal
  • Data Security Policy governed by Data Governance Council
  • Separate Data Security Policy from IT Security Policy (more granular)

Activity 3: Define Data Security Standards

  • Passwords: change every 45–180 days; sufficient complexity; no blank passwords
  • Use two-factor identification for highly sensitive information
  • Assign confidentiality levels to all data elements

Activity 4: Implement Controls and Procedures

  • Implement role-based access control; use Role Assignment Grid or Hierarchy
  • CRUD Matrix — maps access: Create, Read, Update, Delete (some add E for Execute = CRUDE)
  • Manage monitoring: active (real-time) and passive (periodic snapshots)

Activity 5: Audit Data Security

  • Internal or external auditors; auditors must be independent of audited process
  • Not fault-finding — provides objective assessment and recommendations
  • Audit inputs: policy statements, standards, change requests, access logs

14Outsourcing and Cloud Security

Outsourcing Principle: "Anything can be outsourced except liability."

  • Architecture and ownership of security architecture should remain in-sourced
  • Outsourced partner may implement; organization owns/manages architecture

RACI Matrices — define data security responsibilities in outsourcing contracts

Cloud Security:

  • 'As-a-Service' models (DaaS, SaaS, PaaS) require adapted data security policies
  • Chain of custody and shared responsibility critical in cloud environments
  • Business partner use of cloud = organization's data may be in cloud

15Metrics Categories

  1. Security Implementation Metrics — % computers with patches, % with anti-malware, % employees passing security quiz
  2. Security Awareness Metrics — risk assessment findings, feedback surveys, incident post-mortems
  3. Data Protection Metrics — criticality ranking, annualized loss expectancy, vulnerability assessments
  4. Security Incident Metrics — intrusion attempts detected/prevented, ROI for security costs
  5. Confidential Data Proliferation — number of copies of confidential data (reduce this)

16Practice Q&A

Q1: What is the definition of Data Security? A: Planning, development, and execution of security policies and procedures to provide proper authentication, authorization, access, and auditing of data and information assets.

Q2: What are the two primary business drivers for data security? A: Risk Reduction and Business Growth.

Q3: What are the 3 risk classifications? A: Critical Risk Data (CRD), High Risk Data (HRD), Moderate Risk Data (MRD).

Q4: What are the Four A's of security? A: Access, Audit, Authentication, Authorization (plus Entitlement as a fifth, recently added concept).

Q5: What are the 5 confidentiality levels? A: For General Audiences, Internal Use Only, Confidential, Restricted Confidential, Registered Confidential.

Q6: What is the key difference between confidentiality and regulatory restriction? A: Confidentiality originates internally (one level per data set); regulatory is externally defined and additive (multiple categories can apply).

Q7: What is the difference between SOX and Insider Trading Laws? A: SOX restricts who can change financial data (integrity); Insider Trading Laws restrict who can see financial data.

Q8: What is HIPAA and what does it protect? A: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (US); protects Personal Health Information (PHI).

Q9: What is FERPA? A: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (US); protects educational records.

Q10: What are the three main encryption methods? A: Hash (MD5, SHA), Private-Key/Symmetric (AES, DES), Public-Key/Asymmetric (RSA, Diffie-Hellman; PGP is a free implementation).

Q11: What is the difference between persistent and dynamic data masking? A: Persistent = permanently and irreversibly alters data (for non-production environments). Dynamic = changes appearance to user without changing underlying data (for production use).

Q12: What is "In-Flight" vs "In-Place" persistent masking? A: In-Flight = data masked while moving between systems (more secure, re-runnable). In-Place = source and destination same; risks partial data loss if process fails.

Q13: What is a DMZ and what is it used for? A: De-Militarized Zone — area on edge of organization with firewall between it and both internet and internal network; used to pass or temporarily store data moving between organizations.

Q14: What is the "Goldilocks Principle" in data security? A: Data security must be appropriate — not too weak, but not so onerous it prevents users from doing their legitimate jobs.

Q15: What is Penetration Testing? A: Ethical hacker (internal or external) attempts to break into system to identify vulnerabilities before they can be exploited maliciously. Also called "pen test."

HIPAA PHI — Personal Health Information
FERPA Educational records
SOX Restricts who can change financial data
Insider Trading Laws Restricts who can see financial data
PCI-DSS Credit card/financial account data
Encryption: Hash MD5, SHA — integrity verification
Encryption: Private-key AES, DES, 3DES — symmetric
Encryption: Public-key RSA, Diffie-Hellman, PGP — asymmetric

Dynamic Masking Changes display only; underlying data unchanged
